The Jordan River. The world's lowest river, flowing approximately two hundred fifty-one kilometers southward from the mountains of Lebanon through Israel and the Palestinian territories to the Dead Sea. Though relatively modest in length and flow, it holds immense historical and religious significance as a geographic boundary, a baptismal site, and a focal point of Middle Eastern geopolitics.

The Jordan flows from the Anti-Lebanon Mountains south through the Jordan Valley, passing through Lake Tiberias, also called the Sea of Galilee, before reaching the Dead Sea. It is the lowest point on Earth—its mouth at the Dead Sea lies fourteen hundred ten meters, or nearly forty-six hundred feet, below sea level. In Christian tradition, Jesus was baptized by John the Baptist in the Jordan River, making it a pilgrimage destination for Christians worldwide.

The Jordan forms the boundary between Israel and Jordan and historically defined the eastern frontier of ancient Israel. The water level is dropping drastically due to upstream dams and irrigation projects, with the Dead Sea shrinking by about one meter per year. The river is heavily over-allocated. Israel, Jordan, Syria, and the Palestinian territories all depend on its water, leading to chronic conflict. Ancient cities like Jericho, known as the City of Palms, sit near the river and feature prominently in biblical and archaeological records.
